figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Schematic illustration of the four classes of findings through independent variants of a hypothetical equipment-budget task. Matching colors connect selected materials to enlarged inspections; the separate case below illustrates missing information. F1: a benchmark answer contradicts the policy and case. F2: an incorrect benchmark program passes an amount check. F3: a scorer accepts the correct amount with the wrong budget judgment. F4: a target is unsupported when the allocated budget is omitted. The panels do not form an execution sequence.
figures.headline: Four variants of a constructed equipment-budget task each isolate one failure class, from a wrong reference to an evaluator accepting an incomplete decision.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 illustrates the four kinds of failure using a constructed equipment-budget task.

abstract: Policy-based decision benchmarks evaluate whether systems apply written rules to financial and operational cases. Yet a rule-following response can be marked wrong when the benchmark misstates the required decision. We audit nine public policy-based decision benchmarks through source tracing, program execution, and controlled checks. We find unsupported targets, reference errors that survive replay or propagate as solved steps, and evaluators that reject acceptable answers or credit incomplete decisions. To measure the scoring impact, we rescore unchanged model responses. On the 96 LegalBench SARA numeric cases, correcting the scorer raises acceptance by more than 80 percentage points for each of three models, without changing references or responses. In RuleArena Tax, restoring a required zero floor changes 27 of 300 references and narrows an observed model gap. A controlled federal-exemption task with explicit ownership and eligibility assumptions also shows that errors in supplied intermediate answers can affect final decisions. We present BAR (Benchmark Audit and Revision), a versioned collection of audit evidence and revisions for reevaluation.

sections.body: Policy-based decision benchmarks check whether a model applies supplied rules to a case. The paper reports that a released RuleArena Tax reference omits a required zero floor, so a response applying that floor is rejected. It also reports that evaluators can accept responses that omit a required decision. When references serve as solved steps in later tasks, their errors may affect later model decisions. The authors audit nine public benchmarks, rescore unchanged responses, and test whether faulty intermediate answers change new responses. They also release BAR, a versioned set of audit evidence and revisions.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Benchmark defects can mark rule-following answers wrong and can carry errors into later tasks.

sections.body: A task gives a policy P, a question Q, and case information C, and the model returns an amount, a decision, a conditional answer, or an information request. A target is supported only when the visible inputs justify it. Underdetermined decisions are not treated as opposite labels. Nine benchmarks were selected because their inputs, code, or scorers can be inspected. Each finding must give a complete witness, a control or source trace, and an evaluation consequence. Structural counts describe the specified releases. Selected semantic findings do not estimate benchmark-wide error prevalence. Replacement targets must follow from visible inputs or be left unresolved.
sections.heading: Task, selection, and audit standards
sections.headline: Each audited finding is checked against a frozen source release for its policy, inputs, targets, or evaluator.

sections.body: Released reference answers can violate the supplied rules. Restoring the RuleArena Tax zero floor changes 27 of 300 reference answers. OpenExempt's valuation applies each exemption once, and its values are supplied as solved steps. Some DeonticBench programs contain errors yet match the released label. The LegalBench SARA scorer deletes decimal points before extracting an integer. ConditionalQA drops questions with missing prediction IDs from its denominator. A TheAgentCompany budget check accepts replies that omit the required budget judgments. In PolicyGuardBench, 279 groups of identical complete inputs carry conflicting binary labels. These groups give a lower bound of 61 test-label disagreements, which is a consistency bound and not a count of adjudicated errors.
sections.heading: Findings
sections.headline: Defects appear in references, programs, scorers, and targets that the visible policy or case does not support.

sections.body: With inputs and responses held fixed, the Tax zero-floor correction raises accepted answers from 209 to 224 for Haiku 5.5, from 241 to 261 for GPT6 Luna, and from 195 to 220 for Gemma 4 31B, out of 300. The LegalBench SARA parser and exact-zero correction raise accepted answers from 8–9 to 87–91 out of 96. For ConditionalQA, counting missing predictions as zero lowers Answer EM for GPT6 Luna from 52.34 to 47.93 and for Gemma 4 31B from 58.02 to 47.23. In the OpenExempt experiment, revised supplied amounts change accepted answers from 50 to 68 for Haiku 5.5, from 66 to 68 for GPT6 Luna, and from 65 to 64 for Gemma 4 31B, out of 69. Each result comes from one generation per input and condition.
sections.heading: Effects on scores and model responses
sections.headline: Corrected scorers raise accepted answers on unchanged responses, and revised intermediate amounts shift accepted answers unevenly across models.

sections.body: Reference or scorer corrections that keep the policy, question, case, and decision unchanged allow saved responses to be rescored. The Tax zero floor, the SARA numeric parsing and exact-zero rule, and ConditionalQA full coverage belong to this group. Restoring omitted source text or changing the decision problem alters the input and requires new predictions. Examples are a restored missing rule and the minimum-cost objective added to RuleArena Airline. Targets that remain conditional or unresolved, such as OpenExempt valuation candidates, stay under review. Any exclusion-based reevaluation must report original and retained denominators.
sections.heading: Benchmark revisions
sections.headline: Benchmark revisions split into rescoring-compatible corrections, changes needing new responses, and candidates still under review.

sections.body: Prior work documents label errors that affect model selection and MMLU errors found through manual review. HLE-Verified separates verified, revised, and uncertain items. A text-to-SQL audit shows that corrections can change method rankings. BenchGuard, UTBoost, and ELT-Bench-Verified audit agent benchmarks, including instructions, tests, parsers, and evaluation scripts. For policy-based tasks, the paper cites Verma et al. on spurious patterns and follow-up limitations in ShARC. It also cites Nair et al. on the allocation ambiguity in RuleArena Airline. The authors separate effects on scoring from effects on later decisions.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Related audits address label errors and agent evaluators, and a few cover policy-based tasks.

sections.body: The audit finds that responses supported by the supplied policy and case can be rejected, while incomplete decisions can be accepted. Correcting references and evaluators changes measured agreement and observed model differences with responses held fixed. In the amended OpenExempt task, faulty intermediate answers affect later decisions, and revising them affects models differently. Reference replay can show agreement among components that reproduce the same error. BAR keeps audit evidence and versioned revisions for reevaluation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Scores reflect policy reasoning only when inputs, steps, references, and scoring share the same policy and decision requirements.

sections.body: Some checks cover every record in a release. Semantic reviews cover selected cases, use model assistance, and do not involve domain experts. Unflagged records are not necessarily correct, and selected cases do not give a benchmark-wide error rate. The experiments use three models without tools and one retained response per input and condition, so score changes may differ with other models or prompts. The OpenExempt experiment does not fully repair the native task. WorkArena++ and TheAgentCompany checks use constructed inputs and do not measure failure frequency in live runs. TheAgentCompany's budget reference prices remain unverified.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Audit coverage is partial, and experiments use three models with one retained response per input and condition.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the task contracts, selection and verified reuse, inspected populations with their check boundaries, and the review procedure. The review used model-assisted readings without separate human or domain-expert adjudication. Appendix B reports case evidence for RuleArena Tax, NBA, and Airline and for other benchmarks, separating source excerpts from audit calculations. Appendix C gives experimental details, including the OpenExempt input controls and the rescoring results. Some source reviews used Codex without recording its model identifier. The candidate-to-disposition mapping is incomplete, so no rejection rate can be inferred.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists audit scope, inspected populations, source review procedures, detailed case evidence, and experimental controls.
